Questions.A: Let us go into the Presence of God since we now have a way. Let us hold fast to our Christian beliefs and encourage one another to do so.
Questions.Alternative: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer say to the people now? What does he want them to do?
Questions.A: Go right into the presence of God without hesitation.

Questions.Q: What made him think the way was open? // Why was he sure they had the right to go in?
Questions.A: Jesus died to earn them the right.
Questions.Alternative: What made him think the way was open?
Why was he sure they had the right to go in?

Questions.Q: What does it say about the great curtain that was in God's Temple?
Questions.A: When Jesus died, it was torn from top to bottom.

Questions.Q: What kind of curtain was it? // Where did the curtain hang? // What was the curtain's purpose?
Questions.A: It closed off the room where God lived.
Questions.Alternative: What kind of curtain was it?
Where did the curtain hang?
What was the curtain's purpose?

Questions.Q: Is it important that it was torn?
Questions.A: Yes
Questions.Alternative: Is it important that the curtain was torn?
Is it important that the veil was torn?

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because when it tore, the way was opened for people to enter into the place where God lived, into his very presence.
Questions.Alternative: Why was it important that it was torn?
Why was it important that the curtain was torn?

Questions.Q: What else does this verse teach about the way Christ has made it possible for people to enter into God's presence?
Questions.A: It says it is a newly-opened way and one that people can be sure of.

Questions.Q: What does the writer want them to do?
Questions.A: To go right into the presence of God without hesitation or fear that God has not made them completely good.

Questions.Q: Why should they be so bold?
Questions.A: The person in charge there in the place of worship has made it possible for them to go into God's presence and will act on their behalf there.
Questions.Note: See verse 21.

Questions.Q: What else does it tell about the way people are to go in?
Questions.A: They are to go with a sincere heart, sincere desire to come to God.

Questions.Q: What about past sins? How should they feel/what should they think about them?
Questions.A: People no longer need to feel guilty. They have been put away forever.
Questions.Alternative: What about past sins? How should they feel about them?
What about past sins? What should they think about them?

Questions.Q: What does it say about people's bodies, or baptism, or water? // It says that our bodies are washed with pure water. Can you explain what that means?
Questions.A: It says/means people have been baptized to show they have turned from the way they used to live to living to please God.
Questions.Alternative: What does it say about people's bodies, or baptism, or water?
It says that our bodies are washed with pure water. Can you explain what that means?
What do you think it means when it talks about our bodies being washed with pure water?

Questions.Q: Why is he telling them that?
Questions.A: It is another reason they should not be afraid to approach God.
Questions.Alternative: Why is he telling them that their hearts are now clean?
Why is he telling them that they are no longer guilty?
Why is he telling them that they no longer need to feel guilty?

Questions.Q: Now what does the writer tell them [to do]?
Questions.A: Keep expecting God to do what he promised just like they tell other people they believe/expect.
Questions.Alternative: Now what does the writer tell them to do?
Now what does the writer tell them?

Questions.Q: Why does he say people should do that? // How do people know they will receive what he promises?
Questions.A: Because they can trust God to do what he says.
Questions.Alternative: Why does he say people should do that?
How do people know they will receive what he promises?

Questions.Q: What does it say about one another/how people should live with one another?
Questions.A: It says they should be
(1) concerned about one another and
(2) stirring each other up to get involved in showing others that they love them and
(3) and in helping them in every way they can.
Questions.Alternative: What does it say about one another?
What does it say about how people should live with one another?

Questions.Q: What else does he say about the way people should live?
Questions.A: They should not forsake meeting together as some have done.

Questions.Q: What else [does he say about those meetings]?
Questions.A: People should use them to encourage each other to keep on believing in Christ.
Questions.Alternative: What else does he say about those meetings?
What else?

Questions.Q: What does he say about the Return of Christ?
Questions.A: He says the time is getting closer.

Questions.Q: Why did he mention that here?
Questions.A: Since his Return is near, that is even more reason for them to continue meeting and encouraging each other to keep on believing.

Questions.Q: What does Jesus's blood have to do with entering into God's presence?
Questions.A: When he died and shed his blood, he earned for people the right to go into God's presence.

Questions.Q: Why do you think that it tells us that the curtain was torn from top to bottom?
Questions.Note: Here you just want to be sure they don't understand the wrong thing and you may want to tell them why.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: It is a stern warning of what happens to those who turn away from/reject the Son of God.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer say here about sinning?
Questions.A: He says that if anyone sins by rejecting Christ/refusing to depend on his sacrifice as payment for his sins/If anyone deliberately chooses to keep on living evil lives, then there is no other sacrifice to pay for his sins, no way to get rid of them.

Questions.Q: Who is he talking about? Everybody?
Questions.A: Those people who reject Christ after they know what it means to have God forgive their sins.

Questions.Q: If he has no way to get rid of his sins, what can he do?
Questions.A: He can do nothing but live in dread of the terrible punishment when God burns up all his enemies with a raging fire.

Questions.Q: What does it say about those who disobeyed the Laws of Moses?
Questions.A: They were killed without mercy.

Questions.Q: Why is the writer telling them here about those who disobeyed the Laws of Moses?
Questions.A: If those who disobeyed Moses's Laws were punished so severely, how much more terrible will be the punishment of those who treat the Son of God as nothing.

Questions.Q: He treats the Son of God as nothing and does what else?
Questions.A: He says there is nothing special about the blood of Christ.

Questions.Q: What is so special about it?
Questions.A: It made it possible for God to make a New Agreement with people because he accepted it as final payment for their sin.

Questions.Q: This person treats the Son of God and his blood as nothing and what else does he do?
Questions.A: He insults the Holy Spirit even though he is the One who brings God's goodness to people.

Questions.Q: What does this say about God/punishment?
Questions.A: All know he said, "I will punish those who need punishing. I will repay them for the evil they have done."
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about God?
What does this say about punishment?
Questions.Note: For Hebrews 10:30-31, use either the group A questions or the group B questions. It would be redundant to ask all 3 questions.
group A (Heb 10:30-31)

Questions.Q: Who said, "I will punish those who need punishing. I will repay them for the evil they have done"?
Questions.A: God
Questions.Note: For Hebrews 10:30-31, use either the group A questions or the group B questions. It would be redundant to ask all 3 questions.
group B (Heb 10:30-31)

Questions.Q: What does he say is going to happen to evil people?
Questions.A: He is going to punish them.
Questions.Note: group B (Heb 10:30-31)

Questions.Q: What else did he say?
Questions.A: He said he would judge his people.

Questions.Q: What else does it say about God punishing people? // What is it like when God punishes people?
Questions.A: It is a terrible thing to have God punish people in anger.
Questions.Alternative: What else does it say about God punishing people?
What is it like when God punishes people?

Questions.Q: Those people were killed for disobeying. When or under what circumstances were they killed like that?
Questions.A: When there were two or three witnesses to prove the person had disobeyed.
Questions.Note: Use either this question (C) or the following question (D). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question C (Heb 10:30-31)

Questions.Q: If one person reported that someone had broken a law, would the offender be killed? Why?
Questions.A: No. There had to be two or three witnesses to prove that the person had disobeyed.
Questions.Alternative: If one person reported that someone had broken a law, would the offender be put to death? Why?
If one person reported that someone had broken a law, would the offender be killed? Why or why not?
If one person reported that someone had broken a law, would the offender be put to death? Why or why not?
Questions.Note: Use either this question (D) or the preceding question (C). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question D (Heb 10:30-31)

Questions.Q: Why is the writer telling them all this about sinning, punishment, etc.?
Questions.A: He is warning them what will happen if they turn away from Jesus.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: They shouldn't stop believing in Christ. They should remember how strong their faith was at first and how they suffered for being a believer. Now they shouldn't turn back from that because Christ is coming soon and he must find them faithful.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer tell them now? What does he want them to do?
Questions.A: He tells them to remember how it was in the days when they first heard about and began believing in Christ.

Questions.Q: How was it?
Questions.A: People caused them to suffer very much, but they did not stop believing in Christ.

Questions.Q: How did people cause them to suffer?
Questions.A: They insulted them and mistreated them in public.

Questions.Q: What else did the believers do in those early days?
Questions.A: At other times they stood side by side/sympathized with others who were suffering in the same way.

Questions.Q: What else did they do?
Questions.A: They sympathized with those in prison (in prison because of believing in Christ).

Questions.Q: What does it say about their belongings? // What happened to their belongings? How did they feel about it?
Questions.A: They did not get upset when their belongings were taken away from them because they believed in Christ.
Questions.Alternative: What does it say about their belongings?
What happened to their belongings? How did they feel about it?

Questions.Q: Why not?
Questions.A: Because they knew they had much better things in heaven that would last forever.

Questions.Q: Now what does the writer tell them?
Questions.A: He tells them not lose their courage.

Questions.Q: Why not?
Questions.A: Because they will receive a great reward.

Questions.Q: What else does he tell them?
Questions.A: He tells them to be patient.

Questions.Q: In what way?
Questions.A: In doing God's will.

Questions.Q: What does it say about what God promised? What does it have to do with being patient?
Questions.A: If they are patient and continue doing his will, they will receive what God promised to give them.

Questions.Q: What does it say he has promised?
Questions.A: He will come again soon, he will not delay.

Questions.Q: How do we know he promised that?
Questions.A: It is written in God's Book.

Questions.Q: What does he say about his people?
Questions.A: All who live as he wants them to will believe and live, but if anyone turns back, God will not be pleased with him.

Questions.Q: How do we know that he says that about people?
Questions.A: It is written in his Book.

Questions.Q: Does the writer think those he is writing to are among those who turn back?
Questions.A: No

Questions.Q: How do you know?
Questions.A: It says they are not among those who turn back from believing in Christ and will be separated from God forever. They are among those who believe and will live with Christ forever.
Questions.Alternative: How do you know the writer does not think those he is writing to are among those who turn back?
How do you know the writer does not think that?
How do you know the writer does not think he is writing to those who turn back?

Questions.Q: Why is the writer reminding them of how they used to live when they first believed in Christ?
Questions.A: He wants them to continue having courage and strong faith as they did then.

Questions.Q: Give some examples of being insulted and mistreated in public.
It says they sympathized with people in prison, what do you think that means? Why were they in prison?
Questions.A: They were in prison because they believed in Christ.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What is faith // what does it mean to believe God?
Questions.A: (1) It means that people are certain that God will give them everything he has promised.
(2) It also means that people are certain of things he tells them even though they cannot see them.
Questions.Alternative: What is faith?
What does it mean to believe God?

Questions.Q: What do you think are the things we do not see that the author is talking about?
Questions.A: The fulfillment of God's promises: "the good things that are coming" (10:1), forgiveness (10:17-18), God's presence (10:22), eternal possessions (10:34), salvation (10:39).

Questions.Q: What does it say about men in ancient times?
Questions.A: It was because they believed God that he showed them that he was pleased with them.

Section.heading: Hebrews 11:3 Believing that God created the universe

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
How was the world created?
Questions.A: By God's Word. He spoke words/commands and the universe was made.

Questions.Q: Many people do not believe/understand that. Why do Christians understand/believe it?
Questions.A: Because they believe God.
Questions.Alternative: Many people do not believe that. Why do Christians understand it?
Many people do not believe that. Why do Christians believe it?
Many people do not understand that. Why do Christians understand it?
Many people do not understand that. Why do Christians believe it?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does it say about Abel and Cain and the sacrifices they offered? How do they compare? Which was better?
Questions.A: Abel's was better.

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because he believed God.
Questions.Alternative: Why was Abel's sacrifice better?
Why was Abel's sacrifice acceptable?
Why was Abel's sacrifice acceptable to God?

Questions.Q: How do we know Abel's was better? // What happened that showed that Abel's was better?
Questions.A: God did something to show that he approved of Abel's offering.
Questions.Alternative: How do we know Abel's was better?
What happened that showed that Abel's was better?

Questions.Q: What did God think of Abel? // What did God think of the way Abel lived?
Questions.A: He looked at Abel as someone who lived as he wanted him to live.
Questions.Alternative: What did God think of Abel?
What did God think of the way Abel lived?

Questions.Q: Why do you think the author is talking about Abel? // What else does it say about Abel? // What can people learn from Abel?
Questions.A: People can learn from him even though he is dead. They can look at the way he trusted God and learn to obey him.
Questions.Alternative: Why do you think the author is talking about Abel?
What else does it say about Abel?
What can people learn from Abel?

Questions.Q: It says people can learn from him even though he is dead. How? What does that mean?
Questions.A: By hearing or reading about him, people can imitate him.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this say about Enoch? What happened to him?
Questions.A: He didn't die.

Questions.Q: If he didn't die, what happened to him?
Questions.A: God took him away from the earth and nobody could find him.

Questions.Q: Why did he do that?
Questions.A: He was so pleased with him.
Questions.Alternative: Why did God do that?
Why did God take him away from the earth without him having to die?

Questions.Q: What does this say about pleasing God? // If people want to please God, what must they do?
Questions.A: No one can please God unless they believe him/believe what he says.
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about pleasing God?
What does this say about pleasing him?
If people want to please God, what must they do?

Questions.Q: What must they believe?
Questions.A: That he exists and that he rewards those who try to find him.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passages just checked?
Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this say about Noah? What did he do?
Questions.A: It was because he believed God that he was able to hear God's warnings about the future even though he couldn't know what was about to happen.

Questions.Q: What else did he do besides believing God? // What else did he do because he believed God?
Questions.A: He also obeyed him and built a ship in which he and his family were saved.
Questions.Alternative: What else did he do besides believing God?
What else did he do because he believed God?

Questions.Q: What happened to everybody else?
Questions.A: God destroyed them in the water.

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because they did not believe God as Noah did.
Questions.Alternative: Why did God destroy everybody else?
Why did God destroy them?

Questions.Q: And what did God think of Noah? // What did God think of the way Noah lived?
Questions.A: God considered Noah to be a man who lived like he wanted him to because he believed him.
Questions.Alternative: And what did God think of Noah?
What did God think of Noah?
What did God think of the way Noah lived?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: Abraham believed God enough to leave his own country and go live as a stranger in another country.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this say about Abraham?
Questions.A: God told him to leave his country and go to another place which God promised to give him.

Questions.Q: So what happened?
Questions.A: He did it. He obeyed and went even though he didn't know where he was going.

Questions.Q: Why did he do that?
Questions.A: Because he believed God.

Questions.Q: What does this say about Abraham? What happened in the land God gave him? // When Abraham got to that land that God gave him, did he take over?
Questions.A: Abraham lived as a stranger in that land. He did not take it over.
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about Abraham? What happened in the land God gave him?
When Abraham got to that land that God gave him, did he take over?

Questions.Q: What does it mean, he lived as a stranger? How did he live?
Questions.A: He lived in tents, (not permanent houses). (He didn't really have any place to call his own.)

Questions.Q: What about his son and grandson, did they have a permanent house? How did they live?
Questions.A: No, they lived in tents also.

Questions.Q: Do you think they also expected the land to belong to them? Why?
Questions.A: Yes, God promised it to them also.
Questions.Note: Use either this question (A) or the following question (B). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question A (Heb 11:9-10)

Questions.Q: To whom did God promise the land?
Questions.A: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Questions.Note: Use either this question (B) or the preceding question (A). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question B (Heb 11:9-10)

Questions.Q: How did Abraham feel about not having the land for himself?
Questions.A: He waited patiently.

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because he expected God to give him all that he had promised, including a permanent home in that city that God himself designed and built.
Questions.Alternative: Why did Abraham wait?
Why did Abraham wait patiently?

Questions.Q: Explain about this city Abraham expected God to give him.
Questions.Alternative: Ask the respondent to explain about this city Abraham expected God to give him.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passages just checked?
Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: Abraham and Sarah were too old to have children, yet because they believed, they had a son. Abraham had countless descendants.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this tell us about Abraham and Sarah?
Questions.A: Because they believed that God would give them the son he promised them, they did have a son even though both were too old to have children.

Questions.Q: How many descendants did Abraham have? // When it says his descendants were like the stars or sand, what does that mean?
Questions.A: Abraham's descendants were countless.
It would be impossible to count Abraham's descendants, just as it is impossible to count the stars or the grains of sand on the shore.
Questions.Note: If the metaphors of stars and sand are used, be sure the point of comparison is clear.
Questions.Alternative: How many descendants did Abraham have?
When it says his descendants were like the stars or sand, what does that mean?
When it says Abraham's descendants were like the stars or sand, what does that mean?
Why is he talking about stars or sand?
How were Abraham's descendants like the stars or sand?

Questions.Q: It says Abraham was as a dead person when his first child was born, what does that mean?
Questions.A: He was no more able to have children than a dead person.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Section.heading: Hebrews 11:13-16 Waiting for the promise of a heavenly country

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob trusted God all their lives and expected him to give them a place to live in heaven.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this tell about Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, (about the way they lived and died)?
Questions.A: They trusted God all their lives and when they died they were still trusting him.

Questions.Q: Trusting him for what? // What does it mean they were still trusting him?
Questions.A: They were still expecting him to give them the things he promised to give them.
Questions.Alternative: Trusting him for what?
What does it mean they were still trusting him?

Questions.Q: They waited all that time and still they had not received what he had promised?
Questions.A: No.

Questions.Q: Why didn't they just give up?
Questions.A: They knew those things would be given to them some time in the future and were happy thinking about them.

Questions.Q: What did they think about the way they lived here on earth?
Questions.A: They didn't hesitate to tell people they were strangers here.
Questions.Note: Translator may need to reread verse 9.

Questions.Q: If you tell someone you are a stranger in a place, what does that mean? How do you think of the place you are in?
Questions.A: You do not think of the place as your home.

Questions.Q: Did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob then consider the place they had just left to still be their home?
Questions.A: No.

Questions.Q: How do you know?
Questions.A: If they had, they could have gone back there.

Questions.Q: If they did not think of the place where they were living nor the place they came from as their home, where did they consider their home to be?
Questions.A: They longed for a much better place than any here on earth. They wanted to go to a home in heaven.

Questions.Q: What did God think of their idea or what they wanted?
Questions.A: Because they thought like that, God was not ashamed to be called their God.

Questions.Q: So what happened about their home in heaven? // What else did he do for them?
Questions.A: God prepared a home for them in heaven.
Questions.Alternative: So what happened about their home in heaven?
So what happened about their heavenly home?
What else did he do for them?
How was their longing fulfilled?
How was their desire fulfilled?
What did God do about their desire?
What did God do about their longing?

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Section.heading: Hebrews 11:17-19 Abraham trusted God with Isaac

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: It was because Abraham believed God could the raise the dead that he was willing to offer his only son Isaac as a sacrifice.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this tell about Abraham? What did he do? Why?
Questions.A: It was because he believed God that he was willing to offer his only son Isaac as a sacrifice.

Questions.Q: What does it tell about that son Isaac?
Questions.A: God had promised Abraham that Isaac's descendants would be the people God considered to be Abraham's descendants.

Questions.Q: Why was Abraham willing to do it?
Questions.A: He believed God was able to raise dead people to life again, (and therefore could raise Isaac from the dead).

Questions.Q: So what happened?
Questions.A: At the last minute God saved him from dying.

Questions.Q: Why did God ask Abraham to sacrifice his son?
Questions.A: He was testing Abraham to see how much he trusted him.

Questions.Q: It says when God saved Isaac it was as if he had come back from the dead. How would you explain that to someone?
Questions.A: As far as Abraham was concerned, Isaac was as good as dead so that when he didn't have to sacrifice him, it was as if he had come back from the dead.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about Isaac? What did he do? Why?
Questions.A: It was because he believed God that he promised first his son Jacob and then his son Esau that God would give them certain things in the future.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about Jacob? What did he do? Why?
Questions.A: Because he trusted God, he promised Joseph's sons that God would give them certain things.

Questions.Q: When did he do it?
Questions.A: When he was dying.

Questions.Q: What else did he do?
Questions.A: He leaned on his walking stick and worshiped/prayed to/praised God.

Questions.Q: Why do you think it says that he was leaning on his walking stick?
Questions.A: Probably only a reference to his age and frailty.
Questions.Note: The translator just needs to be sure the reader does not understand a wrong meaning.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passages just checked?
Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about Joseph? What did he do?
Questions.A: Near the end of his life, he told his people that when they left Egypt, they were to take his bones with them.

Questions.Q: How do you think that shows that Joseph trusted God? // How does that show that Joseph trusted God?
Questions.A: He trusted God to take his people out of Egypt (and give them the land he had promised their ancestors).
Questions.Note: If explicit in the translation, use the more direct version of the question (i.e., "How does that show...?")
Questions.Alternative: How do you think that shows that Joseph trusted God?
How does that show that Joseph trusted God?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about Moses's mother and father? What did they do? Why?
Questions.A: Because they trusted God, they were not afraid to disobey the king's order to kill all baby boys and hid the baby Moses for three months after he was born.

Questions.Q: That was a great risk. Why were they willing to take it?
Questions.A: They saw that God had given them an unusually beautiful child and trusted that God would keep him from being killed.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: It was because he trusted God that Moses chose to suffer with God's people rather than to stay with the Egyptians. He was thinking of the future.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this tell about Moses? What did he do? Why?
Questions.A: Because he trusted God, when he grew up he refused to be called the son of the king's daughter.

Questions.Q: What did he choose instead?
Questions.A: He chose to be mistreated with the people of God rather than enjoy the short-lived pleasures one gets from doing things God tells us not to do.
Questions.Alternative: What did Moses choose instead?

Questions.Q: Why did he choose as he did? What benefit was there in being mistreated with God's people?
Questions.A: He was looking to the future. He thought it better to suffer for the coming King of God's people than to own all the riches in Egypt.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passages just checked?
Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell us about Moses? What did he do?
Questions.A: He left. He was not afraid to leave Egypt and he was not afraid of the king's anger.

Questions.Q: Why not?
Questions.A: Because he believed/trusted God.

Questions.Q: How much/to what extent did he believe/trust God?
Questions.A: God was so real to him, it was as if he could see God even though God is invisible and he never gave up (trusting him or doing what God wanted him to do).
Questions.Alternative: How much did he believe God?
How much did he trust God?
To what extent did he believe God?
To what extent did he trust God?

Questions.Q: What does this tell about Moses? What did he do?
Questions.A: He established/started the Passover celebration/feast.

Questions.Q: How did he start it? What did they do first?
Questions.A: He told them to kill a lamb and sprinkle the blood on the doorposts of their homes.

Questions.Q: Why did they do that? or What was the purpose of it?
Questions.A: So that the Angel of Death would not kill their oldest sons as he was going to kill the oldest sons of the Egyptians.

Questions.Q: Why was Moses willing? How did he have the courage to tell them that?
Questions.A: Because he believed that God would save his people just like he said he would.

Questions.Q: What do you know about Passover? From what is said here, what do you think it is?
Questions.A: Respondent should understand that it is a celebration of some sort, even thought he may not know the details.

Section.heading: Hebrews 11:29 Faith when passing through the Red Sea

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about the Israelites? What did they do?
Questions.A: They went right through the Red Sea as though they were on dry land.

Questions.Q: Why were they willing to take the chance?
Questions.A: They trusted God to get them safely to the other side.

Questions.Q: What happened to the Egyptians?
Questions.A: When they tried to follow them, they were all drowned.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
What does this tell about Jericho? What happened to it?
Questions.A: The walls fell down after the Israelites walked around them for seven days.

Questions.Q: What made them fall down?
Questions.A: God/the power of God.

Questions.Q: Why did he make them fall?
Questions.A: (1) Because the Israelites believed/trusted him.
(2) So they could go in and take the city.

Questions.Q: What does this tell us about Rahab? What did she do?
Questions.A: She hid the Israelite spies when they came to look at her city.

Questions.Q: Why did she do it?
Questions.A: Because she believed their God was really God.

Questions.Q: So what happened to her?
Questions.A: She did not die with all the others in her city who would not obey God.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: He talks about all the things people have done because they trusted God. Good things happened to some of them and bad things to others, but God was pleased with all of them.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this say about Gideon, Barak, Samson and the others?
Questions.A: It says there is not enough time to talk about them.

Questions.Q: Why did he mention them?
Questions.A: They all trusted God.

Questions.Q: What else did he say about them?
Questions.A: (1) They (some) won wars against kings and whole armies. (33)
(2) They (some) ruled their people justly as God wanted them to. (33)
(3) God gave them (some) what he promised and kept them safe. (33)
(4) even in dens of lions. (33)
(5) God kept them (some) from being burned even in a fierce fire. (34)
(6) God kept people from killing them (some) with a sword. (34)
(7) God made some of them strong again after they were weak and sick. (34)
(8) God gave them (some) great strength in battle. They made whole armies run away. (34)
(9) There were women who trusted God so much he raised their loved ones from the dead. (35)
(10) There were men who were beaten to death because they refused to turn from God and be freed. (35)
(11) Some were laughed at. (36)
(12) Some were beaten with whips. (36)
(13) Some were tied up and put prison. (36)
(14) People killed some of them by throwing stones on them. (37)
(15) People killed some of them by sawing them in two. (37)
(16) People killed some of them with swords. (37)
(17) They wandered about in skins of animals. (37)
(18) They were poverty-stricken. (37)
(19) They suffered from hardships of all kinds. (37)
(20) People mistreated them. (37)
(21) They wandered over the deserts and hills and had no place to live except in caves and holes in the ground. (38)
Questions.Note: Reread and ask, "What else?" as necessary through verse 38 (Note: the answers say "they" but it should be clear that not all of these things happened to all of them.)

Questions.Q: All these bad things happened to them. Why did they happen? // Why did people do those [bad] things to them?
Questions.A: Because they refused to turn from God, to stop trusting him.
Questions.Alternative: All these bad things happened to them. Why did they happen?
Why did people do those bad things to them?
Why did people do those things to them?

Questions.Q: It says that some were beaten to death because they refused to turn from God. Why were they willing to die like that?
Questions.A: They believed that God would raise them from the dead and give them a better life afterwards.

Questions.Q: The writer tells us all kinds of things that happened to those people. What else does he tell us about them?
Questions.A: They were too good for this world.

Questions.Q: What did God think of those people mentioned here?
Questions.A: He was pleased with them.

Questions.Q: Why did the writer just tell all these things about these people, good things that happened to some and bad things that happened to others?
Questions.A: To show how much they all trusted God.

Questions.Q: Besides all the things that happened to them, what else does he tell about them?
Questions.A: They did not receive all the things that God had promised them.

Questions.Q: Why not?
Questions.A: Because God wanted to give them far better things than it was possible to give them at that time.

Questions.Q: What did he want to give them?
Questions.A: He wanted to make it possible for all of them (those who lived back then and people who live now) to become completely all that he wants them to be at the same time.

Questions.Q: Could you explain what you think this verse means?
Questions.A: Many of God's blessings were not available until after the death and resurrection of Christ, such as the indwelling Holy Spirit, the privilege of coming directly into God's presence, etc. Someday all God's people will be made perfect at the same time as the Bride of Christ.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: Since we have so many witnesses as examples for us to follow, let us get rid of everything that hinders us from following the Lord completely and make every effort to live as God wants us to, looking to Jesus as our example.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer tell/want those to whom he is writing to do? What does he say about "things that hinder?"
Questions.A: He tells them to get rid of everything that hinders them from obeying the Lord completely.
Questions.Alternative: What does the writer tell those to whom he is writing to do? What does he say about "things that hinder?"
What does the writer want those to whom he is writing to do? What does he say about "things that hinder?"

Questions.Q: What do all those people just talked about have to do with it? // Why did the writer talk about all those faithful people?
Questions.A: They are examples to people of how they should live/trust the Lord or they are examples of how God gives all he has promised to those who trust him.
Questions.Alternative: What do all those people just talked about have to do with it?
Why did the writer talk about all those faithful people?
Why did the writer talk about all those faithful people in the previous chapter?
Questions.Note: Use either this question (A) or the following question (B). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question A (Heb 12:1)

Questions.Q: Who are the witnesses mentioned here? In what way are they witnesses?
Questions.A: The people mentioned in chapter 11. They are examples to people of how they should live/trust the Lord or they are examples of how God gives all he has promised to those who trust him.
Questions.Note: Use either this question (B) or the preceding question (A). It would be redundant to ask both questions.
question B (Heb 12:1)

Questions.Q: What does it say about a race? What does that have to do with obeying the Lord? // Why is he talking about racing? // What does that mean?
Questions.A: It says just as an athlete makes every effort to win the race he is running so people should make every effort to live as God wants them to.
Questions.Alternative: What does it say about a race? What does that have to do with obeying the Lord?
Why is he talking about racing?
What does that mean?

Questions.Q: He says they are to leave sin/stop sinning. What else does he say about the sin?
Questions.A: He says that it is very hard to stop doing. (It is also attractive and easy to do.)
Questions.Alternative: He says they are to leave sin. What else does he say about the sin?
He says they are to stop sinning. What else does he say about the sin?

Questions.Q: What does this say about Jesus?
Questions.A: People are to trust God as Jesus did and look to him to help them do that.

Questions.Q: Why should he be the one people imitate and look to for help?
Questions.A: He is the one who went ahead of people to show them what it means to trust God and to make it possible for them to trust him to the end.

Questions.Q: How did he/Jesus trust God? // How did he/Jesus go ahead of people? // What did he/Jesus do that shows how much he trusted God?
Questions.A: He was willing to die in a way people considered shameful, i.e., on a cross.
Questions.Alternative: How did he trust God?
How did Jesus trust God?
How did he go ahead of people?
How did Jesus go ahead of people?
What did he do that shows how much he trusted God?
What did Jesus do that shows how much he trusted God?

Questions.Q: Why was he willing to die that way?
Questions.A: He knew God would give him much joy afterwards.

Questions.Q: Where is he now? // Did he give him joy? How do you know?
Questions.A: He is sitting in the place of honor at the right hand of the throne of God.
Questions.Alternative: Where is he now?
Did he give him joy? How do you know?

Questions.Q: It says people are to get rid or everything that hinders them and the sin that trips people up. Can you give some examples of these things?
Questions.A: (1) Anything that distracts people from giving their all to God, love of money, over-involved social life, cares of this life, etc.
(2) Anything that is disobedience to God.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: They are to consider how Jesus endured much suffering to the end and did not give up. They are to be encouraged, after all they have not yet been persecuted to the point of being killed.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer tell them to do?
Questions.A: They are to think about/consider Christ (and him alone).

Questions.Q: What about him are they to consider?
Questions.A: He did not give up trusting God even when men did such terrible things to him and said such terrible things about him.

Questions.Q: Why did he want them to consider these things about Christ?
Questions.A: He wanted them to be encouraged and not give up when they are also persecuted.

Questions.Q: Why should considering Christ's situation encourage them?
Questions.A: Christ's situation was harder than theirs. He had to die because he trusted God and they had not yet been persecuted to that extent.

Questions.Q: How hard was his situation?
Questions.A: He suffered much more than any other human has ever done in his struggle with temptation as he faced death and separation from his Father, and yet he did not give up.
Questions.Note: A respondent will probably only say he died rather than give up.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: He reminds them of God's encouraging words, telling them that the Lord punishes those he loves when they are wrong.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
Who is speaking here?
Questions.A: God

Questions.Q: How do we know he said it?
Questions.A: It is written in his Book.

Questions.Q: Who is he speaking to (or about)?
Questions.A: His children.

Questions.Q: What did he say?
Questions.A: (1) Pay attention/Do not think it is unimportant when the Lord punishes you.
(2) Don't be discouraged when he shows you that you are wrong.
(3) He punishes those he loves.
(4) When he punishes you, it shows that you are really his child.
Questions.Note: Reread and ask, "What else?" as necessary.
For Hebrews 12:5-6, use either the group A questions or the group B questions. It would be redundant to ask all 5 questions.
group A (Heb 12:5-6)

Questions.Q: What does this tell us about God?
Questions.A: God raises his children as a father raises a child.
Questions.Note: For Hebrews 12:5-6, use either the group A questions or the group B questions. It would be redundant to ask all 5 questions.
group B (Heb 12:5-6)

Questions.Q: How is that? // In what sense?
Questions.A: He punishes his child when he/she needs it.
Questions.Alternative: How is that?
In what sense?
In what sense does God treat his people as a father raises a child?
Questions.Note: group B (Heb 12:5-6)

Questions.Q: How should the child react?
Questions.A: Be glad.
Not make light of it or ignore it.
Questions.Alternative: How should God's child react?
How should God's child react to the discipline?
Questions.Note: group B (Heb 12:5-6)

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because God is showing that he loves him/her and that he/she is his child.
Questions.Alternative: Why should the child gladly accept discipline?
Questions.Note: group B (Heb 12:5-6)

Questions.Q: What does the writer say about these words of God? Why did God say them?
Questions.A: To encourage them.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: Endure God's punishment patiently, knowing that he is treating you as a father treats a child he loves. The punishment is for your own good and even though it is hard to take now, later you will be very glad he did it.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this say about suffering/punishment?
Questions.A: Their suffering is God's discipline/training for them. He tells them they are to endure the suffering as God's training for them.
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about suffering?
What does this say about punishment?

Questions.Q: Could you explain that a bit? What else does it say about it?
Questions.A: (1) That's the way every father teaches his children.
(2) When God treats people that way it shows they are his child.
(3) If he does not train/discipline people that way, it shows they are not his children.

Questions.Q: What does this say about our human fathers and God?
Questions.A: It says we respected our human fathers when they disciplined us. How much more we should accept and obey God when he disciplines us.

Questions.Q: If we do accept his discipline, what will happen/be the result?
Questions.A: We will live with him forever.
Questions.Alternative: If we do accept his discipline, what will happen?
If we do accept his discipline, what will be the result?

Questions.Q: What does this say about our human fathers?
Questions.A: They disciplined us for a little while as best as they knew how.

Questions.Q: How is God's correction?
Questions.A: (1) His training is always right.
(2) He trains us so we can become like him.

Questions.Q: What do we learn here about discipline/correction?
Questions.A: We do not enjoy it while it is happening, but when we learn our lesson, we enjoy the peace/rest that comes from living the way God wants us to live.
Questions.Alternative: What do we learn here about discipline?
What do we learn here about correction?

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The writer speaks to them as though they are tired runners in a race and tells them to make new efforts to reach their goal and set good examples for those who come behind them.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the author tell/want them to do here?
Questions.A: To make every effort to reach the goal God has set for them.
He tells them to take a new grip with their hands and to stand firm on their shaky legs.
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them to do here?
What does the author want them to do here?
Questions.Note: Depending on the answer(s) given, ask either the following two questions about the figures of speech used or the next two questions about the meaning/application of those figures of speech

Questions.Q: What does he say about tired hands and shaky legs?
Questions.A: He tells them to take a new grip with their hands and to stand firm on their shaky legs.
Questions.Note: If the respondent gives an answer to the previous question that shows they understand the spiritual application of the figure of speech, use this question and the next question if necessary to ensure the respondent really understands how the figure of speech (about weak hands and knees) relates to their faith.

Questions.Q: Why is he telling them that? Were they weak or sick? What does that have to do with making an effort to reach the goal God has set for us?
Questions.A: He was comparing them to tired runners in a race, about to give up because they were discouraged and about to give up their faith in the Lord.

Questions.Q: What does the author tell/want them to do here?
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them to do here?
What does the author want them to do here?
Questions.Note: If the respondent gives a literal answer to the question about what the author wants them to do, use this question and the next question to ensure the respondent understands the spiritual significance of the instructions.

Questions.Q: b Why is he telling them that? Were they weak or sick?
Questions.A: He was comparing them to tired runners in a race, about to give up because they were discouraged and about to give up their faith in the Lord.

Questions.Q: What, then, is he really telling them to do?
Questions.A: To make every effort to reach the goal God has set for them.

Questions.Q: What does the author tell/want them to do here?
Questions.A: He wants them to be good examples for others who believe in Christ, especially certain ones.
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them to do here?
What does the author want them to do here?

Questions.Q: These others who need their good example, what does he say about them?
Questions.A: They are wavering between following Christ and going back to Judaism.

Questions.Q: If they set a good example for those who are weak, what will happen/be the result?
Questions.A: They will learn to trust the Lord without doubting.
Questions.Alternative: If they set a good example for those who are weak, what will happen?
If they set a good example for those who are weak, what will be the result?

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: He tells them to make every effort to live as God wants them to and to take care that their fellow Christians do the same.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does he say to them/want/tell them to do?
Questions.A: (1) Make every effort to see that each one has that peace/rest in his heart that comes from God.
(2) See to it that each one lives more and more like God wants him to, seeing that he does nothing that would separate himself from God.
(3) Each one should watch out that no one turns away from/rejects/refuses God's offer to rescue them from sin because of what Christ has done for them.
(4) Watch out that no one, by living in such a way that or teaching others things that cause them to turn from God, becomes like a bitter plant that grows up and troubles many with its poison.
(5) Watch out that no one thinks about sex or behaves sexually in any way other than the way God says people should.
(6) Watch out that no one is indifferent to God like Esau.
Questions.Alternative: What does he say to them? (Reread and follow with "What else?" as necessary.)
What does he want them to do? (Reread and follow with "What else?" as necessary.)
What does he tell them to do? (Reread and follow with "What else?" as necessary.)
Questions.Note: Reread and ask, "What else?" as necessary.

Questions.Q: How was Esau indifferent to God? // How do we know Esau was indifferent to God?
Questions.A: He sold his rights as the older son for a single meal.
Questions.Note: How this showed indifference to God is certainly not clear in this passage. It will only become clear if the "rights" he rejected are made explicit. In which case, the following questions should be asked.
Questions.Alternative: How was Esau indifferent to God?
How do we know Esau was indifferent to God?

Questions.Q: How did selling his rights as the oldest son show that he was indifferent to God?
Questions.A: Because he was indifferent to God's promises to the oldest son and his special relationship to God.

Questions.Q: What happened later in regard to that birthright?
Questions.A: Esau changed his mind and wanted the things from God that belong to the oldest son.

Questions.Q: So what did he do?
Questions.A: He begged Isaac, with tears, to give him the blessing.

Questions.Q: What did Isaac do?
Questions.A: He did not give him the blessing.

Questions.Q: What happens to people who are not "holy?"
Questions.A: They will not see the Lord.

Questions.Q: Can you give examples of the things we are not to do?
What was the relationship between Isaac and Esau?
Questions.A: Father and son.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The writer is telling them to think about, or he is pointing out to them, how different the Old Agreement is from the New Agreement. When God gave them the Old Agreement, everybody was terrified.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the writer say about the mountain? What was it like?
Questions.A: It was raging with fire, and covered with darkness, gloom, smoke, and a storm.

Questions.Q: What mountain was it?
Questions.A: Mt. Sinai.

Questions.Q: What happened there? // What happened on Mt. Sinai?
Questions.A: It says their ancestors came to that mountain and there God gave them the laws he wanted them to live by (the Old Agreement).
Questions.Alternative: What happened there?
What happened on Mt. Sinai?

Questions.Q: How did the people feel as they stood near that mountain?
Questions.A: They were terrified.

Questions.Q: The mountain was burning, smoking, etc. What else happened there? // What does it say about a voice and a trumpet?
Questions.A: (1) There was a "bone chilling" blast of a trumpet.
(2) They heard a voice that terrified them.
Questions.Alternative: The mountain was burning, smoking, etc. What else happened there?
What does it say about a voice and a trumpet?

Questions.Q: Whose voice do you think it was?
Questions.A: God

Questions.Q: What did the people say about the voice?
Questions.A: They asked not to hear another word.

Questions.Q: Why does this say they were so terrified?
Questions.A: They were terrified of a God who was so unapproachable that even an animal had to be stoned if it touched where he was.

Questions.Q: What did Moses say?
Questions.A: He said he was trembling with fear.

Questions.Q: What was he afraid of?
Questions.A: He was so awed by the holiness of God that he was afraid of what would happen if they disobeyed God. (See Deut 9:19.)

Questions.Q: Why was the mountain burning, smoking, etc.?
Questions.A: Because God was there. It was a display of his power (to make them afraid to disobey him).

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The writer is telling how different the New Agreement is. The Old Agreement terrified the people it was brought to and they could not come near God at all. But with the New Agreement, they can go right into his presence without fear.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does this say about God or about coming to God? // What difference does this show between the Old and New Agreements?
Questions.A: It says they come to him in a very different way than their ancestors came.
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about God or about coming to God?
What does this say about coming to God?
What difference does this show between the Old and New Agreements?

Questions.Q: How do they come to him?
Questions.A: They come into his very presence.

Questions.Q: Where? Where is he? // Where does this say they come to him?
Questions.A: In his city in heaven, the heavenly Jerusalem, also called Mt. Zion.
Questions.Alternative: Where? Where is he?
Where does this say they come to him?

Questions.Q: Who else is there?
Questions.A: (1) Countless angels.
(2) All those people who are God's children and will receive all the good things he has for his children, all those who have lived as God wanted them to when they lived on earth.
(3) Jesus.

Questions.Q: What else is there? // What does it say about the blood of Christ?
Questions.A: (1) The blood of Christ has been sprinkled there for God to see and forgive their sins.
(2) His blood means something so much better than the blood of Abel.
Questions.Alternative: What else is there?
What does it say about the blood of Christ?

Questions.Q: This says they have come into the presence of God in heaven. What does that mean?
Questions.A: Since they belong to Christ and he is there in God's presence to represent them, when they worship/pray, it is as if they go right into his presence in heaven.

Questions.Q: Why is he telling them about the angels and God's people who are also in heaven? How are they connected with what he is saying here?
Questions.A: When they come to Christ, they become part of this happy group.

Questions.Q: What is this Mt. Zion mentioned here?
Questions.A: It is another name for God's city. (This is probably all they need to know at this point.)

Questions.Q: This says they come to God. What else does it say about him here?
Questions.A: It says he is the Judge of all mankind. He will decide who lived on earth as they should have and who did not.

Questions.Q: This says they come to people who have lived on earth as they should. What else does it say about them?
Questions.A: (1) It says they now have been made completely as he wants them to be.
(2) Their names are written in heaven.

Questions.Q: It says they come to Jesus. What else does it say about him?
Questions.A: It says he puts into operation this New Agreement between God and man.

Questions.Q: It says Jesus's blood was better than Abel's. Why?
Questions.A: Because when God saw it, he felt it was necessary to take revenge on the one who killed him. But when he sees Jesus's blood, he forgives people's sins.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author is telling them that they must pay attention to what God is saying to them because if those people who refused to listen when he spoke to them here on earth did not escape punishment, how much less will they when he speaks to them from heaven.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What is the author telling them now? What does he want them to do?
Questions.A: He says they are to see to it that they obey God. He (God) is speaking to them.

Questions.Q: Why does he say they should do that? What will happen if they don't obey?
Questions.A: He says those people who heard God speaking to them from the mountain here on earth did not escape punishment because they refused to obey him. Now he is speaking to them from heaven and so it is even more sure that they will not escape punishment if they refuse to obey him.

Questions.Q: What else does he say here about God speaking here on earth and his speaking from heaven?
Questions.A: It says when he spoke from the mountain the earth shook, but when he speaks the next time/again, he will speak from heaven and not only the earth, but the heavens will shake once and for all.

Questions.Q: What does he mean when he says he will shake the earth and the heavens once and for all?
Questions.A: It means everything he has created will be shaken and only the things he made to last forever will remain. In other words, the material creation will be removed and he will make everything new and different so that it will last forever.

Questions.Q: It says he spoke to the ancestors from the mountain and now he is speaking to us from heaven. What does that mean?
Questions.A: It apparently means that when he "spoke the first time," gave the Old Agreement, he gave it through Moses, a man of the earth, and when he gave the New Agreement he gave it through Jesus, the Man from heaven. (See 2:2, 3.)
Questions.Note: It is unlikely that any respondent would understand that unless at least part of the implicit information is made explicit.

The translator should be sure that the respondent understands that all the references in these verses to the mountain, Mt. Sinai, etc., are referring to when God spoke to the ancestors of the Jews long ago and gave them the Old Agreement.

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author tells them that since they are a part of a group that cannot be destroyed, they should make use of the gifts and power that are theirs to live in a way that pleases God. And he warns them that God completely destroys all his enemies.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the author say here about the people he is writing to? Who are they? What will they do in the future?
Questions.A: They are a part of the group of people God will rule forever. It cannot be destroyed.

Questions.Q: What does he want them to do?
Questions.A: He wants them to serve and worship God in a way that pleases him with respect and awe.

Questions.Q: How can they do that?
Questions.A: By letting God kindly/graciously help them. In his goodness he enables his people to live in a way that pleases him and he gives them power and gifts so that they can serve him.

Questions.Q: After hearing about this kingdom, explain what you think the previous verse (verse 27) means.
Questions.A: The things that cannot be destroyed are people over whom God rules.

Questions.Q: What happens to God's enemies?
Questions.A: God destroys them as a fire destroys everything in its way.

Questions.Q: Why do you think he is telling them about what God does to his enemies?
Questions.A: He is warning them what will happen to them if they become enemies of God.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author tells them how they should treat each other, namely love each other, welcome strangers, and remember those who are in prison and those who are persecuted.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What is the author telling them here?
Questions.A: He is telling them how they should live.

Questions.Q: What does he say? // How does he say they should live?
Questions.A: (1) They should love each other as people who belong to Christ should.
(2) They should welcome strangers into their homes.
(3) They should remember those who are in prison and those who are mistreated.
Questions.Note: Reread and ask, "What else?" as necessary.
Questions.Alternative: What does he say?
How does he say they should live?

Questions.Q: What does this say about angels? // What else does this say about welcoming strangers into their homes?
Questions.A: It says some who have welcomed strangers into their homes have welcomed angels without knowing it.
Questions.Alternative: What does this say about angels?
What else does this say about welcoming strangers into their homes?

Questions.Q: Can you explain that?
How does this say they should remember those in prison and those who are being mistreated?
Questions.A: They should remember them/help them as they would want people to help them if they were in prison or mistreated.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author continues to tell them how they should live. This time he says married people should be faithful to each other, they should not seek after money, but they should trust the Lord to take care of them.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does he say here about married people?
Questions.A: He says they should keep their promises to each other and never have sexual relations with anyone other than their spouses.

Questions.Q: Why does he say they should do this? What will happen if they do?
Questions.A: Because God will punish those who break his laws about how men and women should live with each other.

Questions.Q: What does he say about money?
Questions.A: He says they must not love money but be content with what they have.

Questions.Q: Why should they be content with what they have? (Don't they need to be concerned about what will happen to them?)
Questions.A: God has promised to take care of them.

Questions.Q: What did he say about it/taking care of them?
Questions.A: He said, "I will never fail to take care of you, I will never leave you without my help."
Questions.Alternative: What did he say about it?
What did he say about taking care of them?

Questions.Q: What does the author tell them here? // Since God has promised to take care of them, what should they do?
Questions.A: He tells them
(1) to be bold/not afraid of what will happen to them and
(2) to say with the singer in God's Book, "The Lord is the one who helps/rescues me when I call him, so I will not be afraid. Man can do nothing to me."
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them here?
Since God has promised to take care of them, what should they do?

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: He tells them to remember how their former leaders trusted the Lord even when they died, and they should do likewise/trust him as they did. After all, he never changes. So stop believing new and different teaching about the Lord.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
It says they are to think about their former leaders. What kind of leaders?
Questions.A: Those who taught them God's Word/gave them God's Message about Christ.

Questions.Q: What does he say about their former leaders?
Questions.A: He tells them to remember/think about consider how they trusted the Lord all their lives and even as they died.

Questions.Q: Why are they to consider them, for what purpose?
Questions.A: In order to imitate them, trust the Lord as they did.

Questions.Q: What does he say about Jesus?
Questions.A: He says he doesn't change. He is the same yesterday, today and forever.

Questions.Q: Why is the author reminding them that Jesus is the same?
Questions.A: (1) They can trust him as the former leaders did, since he is the same now as then.
(2) They must not believe teachings about him that say he is different from what they were taught when they first believed.

Questions.Q: What are these new teachings?
Questions.A: The new teachings say that if people obey rules about what they can and cannot eat, they can believe and obey God better.

Questions.Q: It says obeying rules about what they can and cannot eat does not help them obey God better. Why not?
Questions.A: Sin comes from their hearts. Those rules are outward things that do not change their hearts.

Questions.Q: If keeping rules cannot help people, how can they believe and obey God better?
Questions.A: They are able to believe and obey God better when the Lord in his goodness helps them.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The payment for people's sins was Jesus's death on the Cross. It was a shameful way to die, outside the city. But he was willing to bear that shame to pay for their sins. Now if they who serve him go back to the old ways of keeping Jewish laws because they are ashamed of him, there is no help for them. So let them follow him and bear the shame as he did. After all this world is not their home. Their real home is in heaven.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does he say about an altar/a place were people's sins are paid for/the Cross on which Christ died?
Questions.A: (1) People's sins were paid for by the death of Christ on the cross.
(2) Those who continue to obey Jewish rules to pay for their sins can never be helped by his sacrifice.
Questions.Alternative: What does he say about an altar?
What does he say about a place were people's sins are paid for?
What does he say about the Cross on which Christ died?

Questions.Q: What does this say about where Jesus died?
Questions.A: He died outside the city.

Questions.Q: Why?
Questions.A: Because when the Jewish high priest took the blood of an animal that had been sacrificed and went into God's presence to offer payment for the people's sins, that animal could not be eaten, it had to be burned outside the city. (So Jesus died outside the city so his blood would be acceptable as payment for people's sins.)
Questions.Alternative: Why did Jesus die outside the city?
Why did Jesus need to die outside the city?

Questions.Q: What does the author tell/want them to do?
Questions.A: (1) To go/join Jesus outside the camp.
(2) Be willing to bear his shame.
or
(1) To be faithful/loyal to Christ.
(2) To be willing to do something that others look down on just as he did something considered shameful.
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them to do?
What does the author want them to do?

Questions.Q: What does that mean? // How can they do that?
Questions.A: By leaving the old ways of serving God and being faithful to him/Jesus even if others look down on them.
or
By leaving the old ways of worshiping God and being faithful to Christ even if others look down on them for it.
Questions.Alternative: What does that mean?
How can they do that?
How?
How? In what way?
In what way?
In what way can they do that?
What does that mean to do that?

Questions.Q: The author tells them to bear his shame with him, what shame did he have to bear?
Questions.A: It was a shame to die outside the city (since it meant that the people rejected/hated the person so much they killed him outside the city.) (And only the worst criminals died on a cross.)

Questions.Q: What did they do to Jesus that was considered shameful? Where did they kill him?
Questions.A: They killed him outside the city.
It was a shame to die outside the city (since it meant that the people rejected/hated the person so much they killed him outside the city.) (And only the worst criminals died on a cross.)

Questions.Q: What does this tell them about their home?
Questions.A: This world will not be their home for long, their real home is in heaven.

Questions.Q: Why is the author telling them about their home at this point? How does this fit with what he just said?
Questions.A: They need not be too concerned about what the people of this world think of them. They won't be here long. Their future home is much better than anything here on earth.

Questions.Q: Do you have any other comments to make about the passage just checked?
Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author is telling them how they should live.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What does the author tell them [to do] here?
Questions.A: (1) Praise the Lord without stopping.
(2) Do good.
(3) Share with those in need.
(4) Obey their leaders.
(5) Pray for him.
Questions.Note: Reread and ask, "What else?" as necessary.
Questions.Alternative: What does the author tell them here?
What does the author tell them to do here?

Questions.Q: The author tells them to praise the Lord without stopping. What else does he say about praising him? What is it like? Who is to give it?
Questions.A: (1) It is/is like a gift they offer him.
(2) It is the result/offering of those who claim him as Lord.

Questions.Q: The author tells them to do good and to share with those in need. What does the Lord think about it when they do those things?
Questions.A: He is very pleased when they live that way for him.

Questions.Q: The author tells them to obey their leaders. What else does he say about the work of the leaders?
Questions.A: Their work is to keep watch over the believers and they must give an account to the Lord for the characters of those they are watching over.

Questions.Q: Why does he say the believers should obey them? What happens when the believers do not obey them?
Questions.A: (1) So that the leaders can be joyful when they give their report to the Lord and
(2) So the believers will not be punished.
or
(1) So they can do their work joyfully and not as a burden.
(2) If their work is a burden to them, that would not be to the advantage of the believers.

Questions.Q: The author asks them to pray for them. What does he ask them to pray?
Questions.A: (1) That they will have a clear conscience/(live in such a way) so that they will have no reason to feel guilty.
(2) That they will be able to return sooner to those to whom he is writing.

Questions.Alternative: Do you have any further comments to make about the passage just checked?
Do you have any other comments to make about the section just checked?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author prays for/blesses the readers. He asks the Lord to help them live in a way that pleases Him.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What kind of "talk" is this? What is the author doing? (Is he telling them a story? Explaining something to them? Telling them what to do? Praying for them?)
Questions.A: He is praying for/blessing them.

Questions.Q: What does he ask for them?
Questions.A: 1) He asks that God will give them every good thing they need, to do what he wants them to and
2) That God will give them the help of Christ to make them able to do what pleases him.

Questions.Q: What can they learn about God and Jesus from these verses?
Questions.A: (1) He is the God of peace/the God who gives them rest in every way.
(2) He accepted the blood of Jesus Christ as a payment for people's sins once and for all.
(3) He raised Jesus from the dead to be the supreme head/leader and caretaker of God's people.
(4) He put God's New Agreement into effect.

Questions.Q: What does he say about praise as he closes the prayer/blessing? // How does he close the prayer/blessing?
Questions.A: He says that Jesus Christ is to be praised forever and ever.

How does he close the blessing?

Questions.Q: Briefly tell in your own words what the author said.
Questions.A: The author closes the letter by asking them to pay attention to the letter, telling them that perhaps Timothy and he will visit them soon, and sends greetings to everyone.

Questions.Q: Tell in your own words as much as you can remember.
What is the author telling them now? What does he want them to do?
Questions.A: He is asking them to listen patiently to his advice in the letter.

Questions.Q: What else does he say about the letter?
Questions.A: It is very short.

Questions.Q: What does he tell them about Timothy?
Questions.A: (1) He is out of jail.
(2) If he comes to him soon, the two of them will visit them.

Questions.Q: What does he tell them here? // How does he close the letter?
Questions.A: (1) He sends greetings to their leaders and other believers.
(2) He tells them that the Italian believers send them greetings. and
(3) He asks God to be with them.

How does he close the letter?
